explanation: Light reflects when it hits something and bounces away rather than going through it. We draw an imaginary line called the normal straight out from the spot where the light touches the object. The angle between the incoming ray and the normal is always exactly the same as the angle between the bouncing ray and the normal. Also, the incoming beam, the reflected beam, and that normal line all sit on one flat plane. If the surface is shiny and smooth, like a mirror, we get a clear reflection which is how we see our own face. But if the surface is bumpy, the light bounces off in all directions, which is called diffuse reflection.
label: good

explanation: Reflection is just light bouncing back off a surface instead of passing inside. To measure this, scientists use a normal, which is a fake line standing at 90 degrees to the surface right where the light hits. The key rule is that the angle where the light comes in and the angle where it leaves are equal when measured against that normal. All three parts—the ray going in, the ray going out, and the normal—are on the same plane. When a surface is smooth, you get a clean specular reflection, which allows you to see your mirror image. Rough surfaces scatter the light, which is diffuse reflection, so no clear image.
label: good
